relations.note: The critical epic identifies Ekalavya as Hiraṇyadhanuṣ’s son.
A secondary genealogy makes Hiraṇyadhanuṣ Ekalavya’s adoptive rather than biological father.
An appended genealogy makes Devāśravas Ekalavya’s biological father.

relations.myth: Ekalavya seeks instruction and adopts Droṇa’s clay likeness
relations.note: Droṇa refuses him, but Ekalavya practices before his image and claims discipleship.
Ekalavya cuts off his right thumb and presents it as teacher’s fee.
Arjuna complains that Ekalavya surpasses him, prompting Droṇa’s demand for the thumb.
Ekalavya appears among the rulers attending Yudhiṣṭhira’s royal sacrifice.
Longer recensions assign Ekalavya the service of carrying or presenting footwear.

relations.myth: The princes discover the arrow-filled dog
relations.note: Bhīma is among the princes whose dog reveals Ekalavya’s extraordinary archery.

relations.myth: The princes discover the arrow-filled dog
relations.note: Nakula is among the princes whose dog reveals Ekalavya’s extraordinary archery.

relations.myth: The princes discover the arrow-filled dog
relations.note: Sahadeva is among the princes whose dog reveals Ekalavya’s extraordinary archery.
Later epic notices describe Ekalavya repeatedly challenging Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa kills Ekalavya, removing a warrior later portrayed as threatening the Pāṇḍavas.
An appended Yādava genealogy makes Ekalavya a cousin of Kṛṣṇa.
Ekalavya and Pradyumna exchange arrows and mace attacks in appended battle narratives.
Balarāma fights or strikes Ekalavya in appended Harivaṃśa battle narratives.
Sātyaki appears on the opposing Yādava side; direct contact varies between appended passages.
Later synthesis portrays Ekalavya as Jarāsandha’s ally or subordinate.
